query: For a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy used as a thin coating on a conventional metal substrate, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation during sliding in the intended high-temperature operating regime? Define a controlled change relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the corresponding directional changes in wear and deformation, state the regime in which those predictions should hold, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Incorporating hard particle reinforcements (e.g., TiC particles) into the FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy (HEA) coating will enhance wear resistance and modify microscopic deformation during high-temperature sliding by promoting dispersion strengthening and grain refinement, which in turn inhibit dislocation mobility and crack propagation.
generation.material_initial_state: A FeNiCrCoCu HEA coating deposited on a conventional metal substrate without any particle reinforcement.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled amount (for example, around 20 wt.%) of TiC particles into the HEA coating during its deposition process.
generation.conditions: High-temperature sliding regime (temperatures in the range of approximately 300–500°C, representative of the intended operating conditions) while under controlled sliding load.
generation.structural_mediator: The well-dispersed TiC particles create a fine-grained microstructure and form strong particle–matrix interfaces, which act as barriers to dislocation motion and help arrest crack propagation.
generation.mechanism: TiC particles induce both fine-grain and dispersion strengthening. This causes a reduced mobility of dislocations and limits local plastic flow. Under high-temperature sliding, these microstructural features help transition the wear mechanism toward less adhesive and fatigue-driven modes, thereby reducing wear and microscopic deformation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline (unreinforced coating), the TiC-reinforced coating will exhibit lower wear rates and friction coefficients, along with evidence of suppressed plastic deformation (e.g., fewer deformation twins, lower dislocation densities) under high-temperature sliding conditions.
generation.baseline: FeNiCrCoCu HEA thin coating made without TiC particle reinforcement.
generation.boundary: This predicted behavior is expected to hold under high-temperature sliding conditions (near 300–500°C). Effects may vary if the temperature is significantly outside this range or if sliding speeds and loads deviate considerably from the tested parameters.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvement in wear resistance and the detailed nature of the microstructural changes (e.g., the optimal reinforcement amount and distribution) are uncertain and may depend on the processing conditions and TiC dispersion quality.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeNiCrCoCu HEA coatings with identical deposition conditions: one set without any reinforcements (baseline) and the other with 20 wt.% TiC added. Subject both sets to high-temperature sliding wear tests (e.g., at 300–500°C, under the same load and sliding speed). Post-test, use scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to analyze the microstructure, measuring dislocation densities, grain sizes, and the prevalence of cracking or deformation twins.
measurements: Grain size and dislocation density (via SEM/TEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the TiC-reinforced coating does not display a statistically significant decrease in wear rate and friction coefficient or does not show reduced microscopic deformation (i.e., similar or higher dislocation densities and crack formation) compared to the baseline coating under high-temperature sliding, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Zhang et al. [] prepared a composite powder coating of TC4 and WC on the surface of TC4 titanium alloy. The results showed that adding 5%, 10%, and 15% WC content could help improve the microhardness and wear resistance of the coating, and the coating forming quality was good without cracks and other obvious defects. Chong et al. [] added 5% WC into AlCoCrFeNi high entropy alloy powder, and the research showed that WC enhanced the hardness of the AlCoCrFeNi coating, reduced the surface roughness, and improved the wear and corrosion resistance. Hu et al. used high-speed laser cladding to prepare a Ni/WC composite powder coating. The research showed that WC improves the microhardness and wear resistance of the coating and can refine the grain structure, and the decomposition of C and W elements precipitated from the coating played a solid solution strengthening role. Ma et al. [] studied the microstructure, microhardness, and wear resistance of a 60% WC-reinforced FeCoNiCr composite coating prepared by laser cladding. The results showed that the composite coating had good forming quality and better microhardness and wear resistance.

AbstractAl1.8CrCuFeNi2 high-entropy alloy coatings with different TiC contents were prepared using laser cladding. The effect of TiC on the microstructure, hardness and wear resistance of the coatings was investigated. It was found that the phase structure of the coating with 10 wt.% TiC was a single BCC phase with no other precipitated phase. When 20 wt.% TiC was added, the phase structure of the coating was a BCC phase and TiC phase. When the TiC content increased to 30 wt.%, more TiC-reinforcing phase was formed. With the increase in the TiC content, the hardness of the high-entropy alloy coating was enhanced and the wear loss clearly decreased, which was closely related to the change in the coating structure. The addition of TiC to high-entropy alloys plays the role of fine-grain strengthening and dispersion strengthening.Keywords: high-entropy alloys, wear resistance, coatings, titanium carbide

chosen.approach: Incorporation of particle reinforcements in HEA coatings
